en: You have taken away my every mark and sign, by meeting eyes with me.
You told me a thing beyond reach, by meeting eyes with me.
Making me drink the wine from love's still,
you have made me drunk, by meeting eyes with me.
Fair, fair arms, green, green bangles:
you seized my arms and took me, by meeting eyes with me.
I give myself over and over to you, my dyer;
you have dyed me in your own colour, by meeting eyes with me.
Khusrau gives himself over and over to Nizam;
you have made me a bride, by meeting eyes with me.
You told me a wondrous thing, by meeting eyes with me.
rom: chāp tilak sab chīnī re mose nainā milāike
bāt agam kah dīnī re mose nainā milāike
matvālī kar līnī re mose nainā milāike
gorī gorī baīyāṁ, harī harī cūṛiyāṁ
baīyāṁ pakaṛ har līnī re mose nainā milāike
bal bal jāūṁ maiṁ tore raṅg rajvā
apnī sī raṅg dīnī re mose nainā milāike
khusro nijām ke bal bal jāe
mohe suhāgan kīnī re mose nainā milāike
bāt ajab kah dīnī re mose nainā milāike
notes: Line 1.1: chāp and tilak are the caste and sect marks worn on the forehead: the beloved's glance has erased the singer's identity.
Lines 1.2 and 5.3: agam, beyond reach or understanding, and ajab, wondrous; the "thing" (bāt) is the mystic's secret.
Line 4.1: the dyer (rajvā, rangrez) runs through Khusrau's poetry: the master dyes the disciple in his own colour.
Line 5.1: Nizam is Khusrau's Sufi master, Nizamuddin Auliya of Delhi. The song survives in the qawwali tradition, and singers vary its lines and their order.
